pages.x: For two centuries Japan had kept nearly all foreigners out. In July 1853 four American warships, two of them belching smoke from steam engines, sailed into Edo Bay under Commodore Matthew Perry. He handed over a letter demanding that Japan open its ports, and came back the next year with a bigger fleet. Japan gave in.

The treaties forced on Japan let foreigners trade and live under their own laws, and many samurai were furious with the shogun, the military ruler, for giving way. Under the slogan revere the emperor, expel the barbarians, young samurai from the domains of Satsuma and Chōshū attacked foreigners and plotted against the shogun.

In 1867 the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, handed his power back to the emperor, hoping to keep his lands. Early in 1868 the samurai of Satsuma and Chōshū declared the emperor's rule restored and beat the shogun's forces near Kyoto. The emperor was a boy of 15; his reign was named Meiji, enlightened rule.

The young emperor moved from Kyoto to the shogun's city of Edo, renamed Tokyo, the eastern capital. In his name the new leaders promised to seek knowledge throughout the world. In 1871 they abolished the lords' domains, and within a few years the samurai lost their pay and their right to wear swords.

In 1871 nearly half the government set off on a long tour of America and Europe, the Iwakura Mission, to study everything from schools to shipyards. Japan built railways, telegraphs, factories and an army of conscripts, took up Western clothes and the Western calendar, and sent every child to school. The first railway ran from Tokyo to Yokohama in 1872.

Saigō Takamori, a giant of a Satsuma samurai, had helped lead the restoration, but he came to hate what the new Japan was doing to his class. In 1877 thousands of samurai rose with him. They were crushed by the new army of conscript farmers, and Saigō died at Kagoshima. Japan still loves him as the last true samurai.

In 1889 the emperor gave Japan a constitution, modelled on Germany's, with an elected parliament but great powers kept for the throne. It was written by Itō Hirobumi, Japan's first prime minister. Within a few years Japan had beaten China in a war, and in 1905 it would beat Russia.

In a single lifetime Japan went from a closed land of lords and samurai to an industrial power with an empire of its own, one of the few Asian countries never colonised. Its success inspired reformers across Asia, but the army and the empire it built led it on to war with China and, in the end, the Second World War.
